newsitem.title: TAIWAN: Taiwan fishermen rally against Japan in island row.
newsitem.headline: Taiwan fishermen rally against Japan in island row.

text.p: Taiwanese fishermen hurled rotten fish at Japan's Taipei visa office and burned Japanese flags on Thursday to protest against Tokyo's expulsion of Taiwan fishing boats near a disputed chain of East China Sea islands.

Shouting "Japanese dogs, get out!" and wielding banners that read "Against Japanese pirates", some three dozen fishermen and opposition politicians demanded Japan halt all activities asserting sovereignty over the Diaoyu islands.

A long-dormant dispute over the Diaoyus, called the Senkakus in Japanese, erupted in July after the right-wing Japan Youth Federation erected a lighthouse on one, angering rival claimants Taiwan and China.
The row intensified in recent days after Tokyo, effectively supporting the rightists, sent patrol ships to repel private Taiwan vessels that tried to approach the islands.
The row has touched off anti-Japanese protests in Chinese communities in Hong Kong, Macau, Taiwan and mainland China.
A group of Taiwan ex-convicts announced on Thursday the formation of a "dare-to-die" force, saying they were willing to carry out suicide missions against the Japanese patrols.
"Six members expressed their determination to die during such a mission," the China Times Express reported, adding that no such operations actually had been planned.
While the Taipei protesters were united in their hostility towards Japan, they nevertheless clashed among themselves on whether Taipei should solicit help from longtime rival China to counter Tokyo.

Fishermen from two political parties scuffled during the rally after one group played communist China's national anthem, which is rarely heard on the island though not banned by Nationalist-ruled Taiwan's exiled Republic of China government.
Taipei reiterated on Thursday that it would not cooperate with Beijing to solve the dispute.
Some residents feel Taiwan and China, separated since the Chinese civil war ended in 1949, should act in concert on their common interest of ousting Japan from the Diaoyus.
Beijing and Taipei agree the islands have been China's for centuries and dispute Tokyo's claim, which dates to China's forced cession of Taiwan and the Diaoyus after its defeat by Japan in 1895.
Both have denounced Japan's support of the rightists' activities and demanded that the Japanese leave the Diaoyus, yet both have resisted mounting popular pressure for a military response.

"The Republic of China advocates resolving the Diaoyu dispute in a peaceful, rational fashion," government spokesman Su Chi said on state television. "We do not consider cooperating with communist China to resolve this dispute."
Taiwan has demanded that Japan stop hindering its vessels near the Diaoyus, but, like China, it has declined to send military patrols to escort or defend them.
Seeking to resolve the dispute through diplomatic means, Taiwan's foreign ministry has said it was ready to negotiate with Japan over fishing rights in waters near the islands.
